properties.name: Parkeren Zoeken?

description.value: 1. The cellar of this house is where Peiper tried to make a deal for POW exchange with ranking US POW, Maj Hal McCown. McCown had no such authority, he said, and was taken along on the German breakout as hostage. McCown's after action report provides valuable information on most of Peiper's trek from La Gleize to Wanne.

This large complex was full of men and tanks during the Ardennes offensive. The panoramic view and post-war lack of renovations are striking . US tanks were picked off as they came down the incline visible to the east. Peiper's men and tanks were also encamped at the Marechal mill where the Werimont road meets the highway, to the east of Werimont. Peiper's column bore right at the Werimont farm and descended to the river.

properties.name: La Venne
properties.description: At around 0430 in this tiny settlement, Peiper picked two men at the Legro farm, Leonard Gason and Yvan Hakin, to guide his column across the river and through the forest. Hakin was interviewed by British author/historian Major General Michael Reynolds later and provided one of four existing eyewitness accounts of the breakout.

description.value: After crossing the river on a footbridge, Peiper's column may have followed the main logging road that switchbacks up the hill, though he preferred lesser-used paths. The road bears right after the river crossing and starts climbing.

properties.name: Waiting Out the Day
properties.description: Peiper avoided the roads and larger paths to avoid detection. During the day of 24 Dec, the main group remained in the deep gully called Trou des Mouchettes, east of Beauloup. Skorzeny scouts dressed as Americans were welcomed in Beauloup, so the group avoided the tiny village. Karl Wortmann reports a spontaneous chorus of Silent Night just before an American sortie flew over. Maj McCown said he accompanied Peiper and his staff on a route recon during the day, in an attempt to rejoin German forces. The ravine is deep but the slope and sides are gentle enough for fairly easy access at both the bottom and top. Stoumont and Cheneux are visible from the open meadow at the bottom left.

description.value: This is an approximate spot based on blow-ups of a map in the 1.SS-Pz.Div. unit history by Ralf Tiemann. Maj Hal McCown described Peiper as almost giddy as the sky cleared. During this portion of the march, Peiper pointed to a frosty tree and told McCown "I promised I would get you a Christmas tree - there it is". Destruction of vehicles left in La Gleize started at 0500 or 0600 by KP men left behind. The clear skies meant the column had to hide under trees to avoid aerial detection.

properties.name: Coo Bridge is Blown
properties.description: Somewhere near this panoramic spot Peiper hoped to drop down east and cross the Amblève over the Coo Bridge. Sounds of a battle could be heard and Peiper hoped it was Kampfgruppe Hansen coming to his rescue. But through his binoculars, he could see that the Coo Bridge - his escape route back to his lines - had been blown by the 105th CEB and that US forces occupied Brume. Then a US column was spotted on a forest road. The 800 men waited in the forest. There was nothing to do but circle back west.

description.value: The column moved out from the ravine just before dark on 24 December. They had been without food or drink since 0100, and from here had to skirt the reservoir and start downhill. One account reports it was "most strenuous", and the column was sometimes single-file. Maj McCown and the two Belgians were still with the column. The exact route between here and the highway is unknown, but the column stayed west and south of Brume as far as the roadside chapel up ahead.

MG Reynolds says Peiper's column passed this "Calvary de la Croisette" roadside chapel before dropping into the forest. A narrow road leads down into the forest directly opposite the chapel, a possible route as there is no cover otherwise available. The panoramic view from here extends for miles north, east, and south.

The column completed their steep descent from the Calvary de la Croisette into the area of Henri Moulin. MG Michael Reynolds reports the route came down the "steep slopes of the Bois de Toirbaileu toward the tiny hamlet of Henri Moulin". One report places them slightly west of Henri Moulin when they crossed the highway in groups, so they may have followed the forest line and/or streambed a little west of Henri Moulin. Karl Laun's group became separated and likely circled farther west along the edge of the forest, passing east of Basse-Bodeux. The location of the brief firefight in this area is unknown - but was close enough to the hill that the men retreated back up the trail when the firing began.

properties.name: A firefight and the Belgians escape

description.value: Somewhere along this stretch of highway, most likely between this intersection and the farm complex slightly west, the long column crossed the highway in small groups. US patrols on the highway fired at some groups and the two Belgium guides took this opportunity to escape into the forest. Several small groups became separated from the main column in the dark. One report states Peiper seemed to be lost and "continuously consulted his map.

Karl Wortmann revisited this area in the 1970's, and recognized the farm as near where he crossed the highway. The farm family remembered hearing the Henri Moulin firefight. The exact location is unknown as Wortmann didn't indicate if he crossed west or east of the farm.

All that's known of the route between the highway and the forest is that Peiper avoided roads and villages. It was rough going with small streams, and "continuously up and down rugged hills." which matches the terrain along the streambed today. After almost 24 hours, the men were lagging as they headed back uphill, and there were rumors that stragglers would be shot. A small path runs along each side of the stream.

Based on US hostage McCown's report, Maj Gen Reynolds believes it was in this area that the German point pushed into US lines three times and turned back, near Saint Jacques. Karl Laun reports seeing a "giant castle" that is perhaps an abbey, but notes US vehicles and a challenge from a sentry. Just as Laun described, the village and church suddenly pop into view when the top of the hill is accessed via the streambed.

At 0100, US Maj McCown reported being between "the village and the west", probably meaning Bergeval. An outpost and aid station of the 517th PRCT was located at the edge of the village directly south of this point. The family Gaspar in Bergeval reported they heard gunfire from between the highway and the river - likely the firefight during which McCown escaped. A path along the forest edge rims this open meadow and crosses the highway.

properties.name: One more uphill before the River
properties.description: A clear path runs along the forest edge just west of this point, crosses the highway, and then drops into a deep stream bed. On the other side, the terrain rises steeply again and ends above the river and rail bed. This area would have been difficult to traverse in the dark and snow.

description.value: Many men by now were asleep on their feet, strung out in the forests north of Bergeval. Either of the two forests road here at the "Y" intersection lead east to the crest of the hill, and then to the switchbacks which descend to the river. The northern route more closely matches the most likely river crossing location. McCown was probably still with the group here.

properties.name: McCown's Escape
properties.description: Another firefight broke out just as they settled for a rest. McCown made a right angle turn toward the fire and successfully rejoined American forces around 200-300 yards away. McCown was no longer near the front of the column at this point. One report says the US troops were close enough to the river to hear the water, so the location may be yet farther east - perhaps even on the downslope toward the river.

description.value: According to Wortmann: "We then had to make our way over stones that some hearty comrades had lain in the ice-cold water. A human chain was assembled, and each man was pulled by the next, stone by stone, sometimes waist-deep in water, to the far bank. Day was already dawning as the last man reached the other bank." Other narratives say the water was chest deep.

After crossing the river, the men had to avoid the every 30 minute US patrols which passed along the road. They would wait until the Americans passed and then dash the "few hundred meters" in the direction of Grand Halleux to the path which ascended up to Div HQ in Wanne.

Karl Wortmann reports that once they were 100 meters above the road, they couldn't resist waving their caps and shouting "Merry Christmas" to the next US patrol that drove down the road. The path breaks out into the open with a clear view of the highway at about this point.

One 6th Company German veteran confirmed that Peiper's men entered Wanne on the road which goes to Aisomont. He was billeted in a farm at this location which is now gone, and watched the frozen column finish their 30+ hour trek. Decades later, the veteran expressed profound relief he had not been with Peiper.

Arriving a little before the rest of the column, Peiper and his command collapsed in exhaustion after reaching the chateau in Wanne. One said "When we reached the village, we were lost souls". Peiper had been lightly wounded in the hand during the firefight across the river, and fell into an 18 hour sleep. By the time he and his men awoke, Christmas was over.
